chapter_theme: The end of the debate with the Buddha: Neelakesi takes apart his balance-beam image of cause and effect and the claim that wholes are only names, asks who reaps a deed's fruit, meets his answer that the reaper is neither the doer nor another but another in the doer's line, like paddy and cane, and argues that what is not the same is other, that his own gifts in former births would then be fruitless, and that the doers reap; he falls silent, assents to the Jain account of things as perishing in one respect and not in another, and she leaves saying that any being who understands the Lord's scripture reaches release.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddha, whom Neelakesi debates in person in this sarukkam; here named by his former gifts (641)
the Buddhists as a body, whom Neelakesi challenges to come in companies (655)

635.reading: Neelakesi tells the Buddha that to anyone who enters into it, all his scripture is like a children's nonsense rhyme about a wasp and a blind oil-woman who poured out her oil for fear her looks would be spoiled.
635.nuance: The rhyme is quoted as a sample of nonsense, not for its content; the insult opens the last round of the debate by calling the whole scripture incoherent rather than one tenet false.

claims.claim: the Buddha's scripture, examined closely, does not hold together

636.reading: Neelakesi takes up the Buddha's image of the balance beam, whose two ends sink and rise at once, and says that if he granted arising and perishing to one gathered whole in the same way she would call it fitting.
636.nuance: The beam is the Buddhist image for a cause ceasing as its effect arises; her point is that the image needs one beam, a single thing that bears both motions, which is what the doctrine of momentary aggregates denies.

claims.claim: the cause ceases as the effect arises, like the two ends of a balance beam
arising and perishing need one continuing thing to happen in, as the beam's ends need the beam

637.reading: If he answers that the beam has no standing of its own apart from the sinking and rising of its ends, and that its oneness is only a name given by convention, she tells him to hear the many faults that follow.
637.nuance: இடுகுறி, an assigned name, is the Buddhist account of every whole as a label for parts; the faults are given in 638 and 639.

claims.claim: the beam is one only by an assigned name; nothing stands besides the motions of its ends

638.reading: If beam and ends do not exist together, she says, she has answered that already, and a further fault follows: he would have to say there is a cow that gives milk without tail, head or middle.

claims.claim: the whole and its parts do not exist together
a whole that does work cannot be denied while its parts are granted

639.reading: If he says compounded things are unreal yet grants that the awareness of them is real, she argues, he falls into the tangle of quality and bearer, part and whole, and has brought that great trouble on himself.
639.nuance: Line 1's சொன்னேற்கு is first person and does not fit the sense well; the reading takes the line as stating his position.

claims.claim: compounded things are unreal though the cognition of them is real

640.reading: Two masses, three masses, countless masses, and more to come: she bids him leave them, take one whole and set the soul's good in it, and so act as one blessed.
640.nuance: பிண்டம் is a lump or aggregate; she mocks the multiplying of momentary heaps and urges a single bearer of the self's welfare. The last line is hard to construe.

claims.claim: the soul's good needs one enduring bearer, not a series of aggregates

641.reading: When Neelakesi asks whether the doer of a deed enjoys its fruit, or another, or all, or no one, the one who had given his eyes more times than the sea has grains of sand begins to answer.
641.nuance: The Buddha is named only by his gifts in former births (eyes given beyond counting), the very gifts she will turn against him in 649 and 653.
641.event: Neelakesi asks the Buddha who reaps the fruit of a deed, and he begins his answer.

642.reading: The Buddha says he does not call the reaper the doer, nor another, nor both, nor can it be said no one reaches the fruit, and bids her hear who it is.
642.nuance: A fourfold denial; Neelakesi answers it in 645 to 651 by holding that what is not the same must be other.

claims.claim: the one who reaps a deed's fruit is neither the doer, nor another, nor both, nor no one

643.reading: He says it is neither that, nor other, nor both, nor like it, but another thing arising in its line, and offers an example.
643.nuance: The key words are அதன் வழியின் மற்றொன்று, another in its line: the doctrine of a continuity without identity, which 646 and 651 attack.

claims.claim: what bears the fruit is neither the same nor other but another in the same line of continuity

644.reading: It is not the seed sown, nor the sprout, nor what came from those two, he says, but as with tall sweet sugarcane and paddy; and he bids the fair-browed woman look at it from the middle.
644.nuance: நடுவாக நோக்காய் asks her to look from the middle, the Buddhist middle between identity and difference; Neelakesi takes his own paddy and cane apart in 650 and 651.

claims.claim: as with paddy and cane, the later growth is neither the seed nor other than its line

645.reading: Neelakesi says that if it is not the same it is other, and she sees nothing he has established; as a horse that is not male is a mare, can he prove anything that both is and is not so?
645.nuance: She presses the excluded middle against his tetralemma; the first two lines are hard to divide.

claims.claim: what is not the same must be other; there is no third case

646.reading: Whether by resembling the doer, by not being him, by coming in his line, or by being called other, she asks, is there any way the reaper ceases to be another?

claims.claim: resemblance and descent do not make the reaper the doer; he remains another

647.reading: Though a carp is like an eye, though a thicket is not a forest, though things multiply through the female, all of them are other things.
647.nuance: Three examples answer his three ways in 646: likeness (the carp and the eye), being less than the whole (thicket and forest) and descent (offspring); each still yields another thing. The verse is in short lines, unlike its neighbours.

claims.claim: likeness, partiality and descent each leave the thing another

648.reading: She says he holds that a stranger reaps and the doer does not, and calls this a heaping up of impossible things, like describing a creature that is no hare, faintly like one in the face, like a field-tortoise.
648.nuance: The run of comparisons in lines 2 and 3 is obscure (மக்குளி is not clear); their sense as a list of impossibles is taken from line 4.

claims.claim: on the Buddhist account another reaps what the doer did, and the doer never reaps it

649.reading: If the reaper is neither another nor himself, and so is another after all, she asks the Buddha who took birth as a hare: if the one who did the deed gets no fruit of it, what is that fruit but waste?
649.nuance: The hare birth is the tale of the hare that gave itself as food; she does not deny the tale here but uses it: on his doctrine its fruit could never have reached the Buddha. Line 2's address to a woman of cloud-dark tresses suggests line 1 quotes his formula back at her.

claims.claim: if the doer gets no fruit, the Bodhisattva's self-giving in former births gained him nothing

650.reading: He likened it to paddy, other than itself yet not other, but then said something else; when he tells of those in heaven, she asks, is not the one who gains heaven another than the one who earned it?
650.nuance: Line 1 is hard to construe; the force is that his own preaching of heaven as a reward needs the one rewarded to be the one who did well.

claims.claim: on the Buddhist account the one who reaches heaven is other than the one who earned it

651.reading: Let him say that sugarcane comes in the line of paddy and paddy from cane; if he cannot, his example fails, and if he says the son in the line of the father who did the deed is not the father, his account comes apart.
651.nuance: She turns his paddy against him: paddy gives only paddy, so the example shows a kind that persists, not a 'neither same nor other'. The last words (உலங்கருவாமே) are obscure.

claims.claim: seed gives its own kind, so the paddy example proves sameness of kind, not a reaper who is neither same nor other

652.reading: The Buddha says the doer is the doer and the reaper the reaper and that this is how his truth lies; Neelakesi asks whether others reach the fruit, saying the fruit of both kinds of deed belongs to the doers themselves, and he sits silent in thought.
652.nuance: His new formula keeps doer and reaper as two terms, which grants her the separation she has been pressing; her answer, செய்தார்கள் தாம், makes the doer the reaper. His falling silent is the turn of the debate.
652.event: The Buddha restates that doer is doer and reaper is reaper; Neelakesi answers that the doers reap, and he falls silent.

claims.claim: the doer is only the doer and the reaper only the reaper
the fruit of good and bad deeds alike falls to those who did them

653.reading: She reminds him that in former times he toiled only for others, giving eyes, head, flesh and wife, and asks whether, even now, he has failed to teach any way by which the doers of a deed come to eat its fruit.
653.nuance: The gifts Kundalakesi praised (205) become evidence against the Buddha: they were made in hope of fruit, and his teaching leaves no one to receive it.

claims.claim: a teacher who gave his body in former births for its merit must account for how the doer reaps

654.reading: However much he strains and however long he ponders, she says, if he claims by his own vision to explain how a deed joins its fruit, let him see that it comes to not even a millet grain.
654.nuance: காட்சி may mean his view or doctrine as well as his seeing; either way the verdict is that the doctrine cannot join deed to fruit.

claims.claim: the Buddhist doctrine cannot join a deed to its fruit at all

655.reading: Unless he wants total destruction, what stood before must continue, and if it slips away that contradicts his own word; she challenges the Buddhists, however many, to gather in their companies and defend their tenet.
655.nuance: The choice she gives is annihilation or persistence; the challenge to all Buddhists widens the debate from the Buddha to his order.
655.event: Neelakesi challenges all the Buddhists to come together in companies and defend their tenet.

claims.claim: unless one accepts total annihilation, what existed before must persist

656.reading: Quoting his objection that a thing which stays is eternal, one which ceases is not, and one called both has the faults of both, she asks whether by saying so he makes himself a one-sided thinker.
656.nuance: ஏகாந்தன் is the Jain word for one who holds a single-sided view; the charge turns his objection to the Jain 'both' into evidence of his own error. The answer is given in 657.

claims.claim: to call a thing both lasting and passing incurs the faults of both
refusing a thing's being both lasting and passing in different respects is one-sidedness

657.reading: When she asks whether he will not praise a conclusion in which a thing is cut off in one way, not cut off in that way too, and both, a conclusion that is no false cutting, the Buddha says he will praise it.
657.nuance: உச்சேதம் is annihilation; the Buddha here assents to the Jain many-sided account he attacked in 656. Whether line 4 gives her question and his assent, or his challenge and her assent, turns on the masculine என்றான், which favours the Buddha as speaker.
657.event: The Buddha agrees to praise the Jain conclusion that a thing perishes in one respect and not in another.

claims.claim: a thing is annihilated in one respect, not annihilated in another, and both

658.reading: Neelakesi says that those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach in due order the release they seek; bidden to go on with steadfastness, by scripture or another way, she departs.
658.nuance: எவ்வுருவினாரும், those of any form, includes the speaker herself, a demoness converted (4). முறையினால் makes release gradual, by order, not sudden. Who says செல் in line 4 is not stated; the Buddha is the likeliest.
658.event: Neelakesi tells the Buddha that anyone who understands the Lord's scripture reaches release, and having won, she leaves.

claims.claim: whoever understands the Lord's scripture, of whatever form, attains release in due order

links.note: In 574 the Buddha said deed and fruit exist but there is no doer; asked now who reaps, he gives a fourfold denial: not the doer, not another, not both, not no one.
links.teaches: Pressed on the reaper rather than the doer, the no-doer thesis has to become a tetralemma, so the denial of a self costs the Buddha the power to name who receives karma.

links.note: In 574 the Buddha denied any doer; here he says the doer is the doer and the reaper the reaper.
links.teaches: Neelakesi's pressure forces the Buddha from 'no doer' to 'the doer is the doer', which is the point at which she can make the doer the reaper and he falls silent.

links.note: The Buddha offered paddy and sugarcane as a continuity that is neither same nor other; Neelakesi answers that paddy never comes from cane's line, so the example shows each kind giving only itself.
links.teaches: The seed example cuts both ways: what the Buddhist uses to show change without identity the Jain uses to show a kind that persists, so the dispute is over which feature of the seed counts.

links.note: The Neelakesi's Buddha says the reaper is neither that nor other; the Manimekalai's teacher draws from the nayas a middle that is 'neither that nor what is not that' (அதுவும் அன்று அது அலாததும் அன்று), and that there is no doer apart from the doing.
links.teaches: The formula the Jain poem gives the Buddha is the one the Buddhist epic itself teaches, so Neelakesi's excluded-middle reply in 645 strikes the school's own middle way, not a caricature.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher calls 'paddy seed gives paddy sprout' the naya of own-nature; Neelakesi uses the same fact, that paddy gives only paddy, to argue that the Buddha's example proves sameness of kind.
links.teaches: One observation serves the Buddhist as a law of causes without a self and the Jain as proof of a persisting kind, so the two epics agree on the fact and differ on what it shows.

links.note: Kundalakesi listed the Buddha's gifts of eyes, flesh, wife and body as his glory; here Neelakesi lists the same gifts to ask how, on his doctrine, he could ever reap them.
links.teaches: The Jataka gifts are turned from praise into a refutation: if no doer reaps, the Bodhisattva's sacrifices were made for a fruit his own teaching denies him.

links.note: Mokkalan raised the faults of holding a thing both to stand and to perish; the Buddha now makes the same objection, and Neelakesi calls it one-sided.
links.teaches: The same objection recurs from the disciple to the master, and the reply sharpens from 'each in its respect' (378) to the charge of ekanta, naming the error the Jain sees in every Buddhist objection.

links.note: In the Manimekalai the Jain's account of things as lasting and passing at once is heard and left among the doctrines Manimekalai sets aside; in the Neelakesi the Buddha himself is made to praise that account.
links.teaches: Each epic stages the same Jain doctrine before the other side and gives it the opposite fate, so the debate scenes show how each school wanted the meeting to end.

links.note: The opening called Neelakesi a demoness who took the great one's dharma and turned from violence; her last words say those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release.
links.teaches: Her closing claim generalizes her own story: a demoness who learned the scripture is the proof that form and birth do not bar release.

links.note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi makes 'the doers themselves reap' the point that silences the Buddha.
links.teaches: The proverb that a deed finds its doer turns out to presuppose a doer who lasts until the fruit comes, which is exactly what the Buddhist no-self denies and what Neelakesi defends.

gains.a: the debate's decisive answer gets a common-sense image of karma that ordinary hearers already trusted
gains.b: the quatrain's untroubled image is shown to carry a metaphysical premise, a persisting self, that one school rejects

links.note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back to oneself in the afternoon, of themselves; Neelakesi argues that the fruit of deeds falls to the doers themselves (செய்தார்கள் தாம்).
links.teaches: The couplet's 'to oneself' (தமக்கு) is set within one day of one life, while the debate asks whether the same self is there across births to receive it.

gains.a: Neelakesi's claim gets an ethical rule everyone grants, so its denial looks like a denial of morality itself
gains.b: the couplet's returning harm is stretched across births, where the identity of the one it returns to becomes a question

links.note: Kural 356 says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return; Neelakesi says those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release in due order.
links.teaches: Both make understanding the road to release, but the epic names whose scripture it must be and adds that any being, even a demoness, may walk it, by stages.

gains.a: the epic's sectarian claim is set beside a general rule that learning and seeing truth free one from birth
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'true thing' is claimed by one school's scripture, and its learner is opened to beings of any form

links.note: Tirumular says souls that know what truly is go to grace and release is becoming one with Siva; Neelakesi says understanding the Lord's scripture brings release in due order, with no grace and no union.
links.teaches: Both put knowledge first, but in the Saiva verse knowledge leads to grace and union with God, while in the Jain verse the Lord gives only the scripture and the soul reaches release by its own understanding.

gains.a: the Jain claim is sharpened by a rival account that needs grace and union where it needs neither
gains.b: the Saiva sequence of knowing, then grace, then union, stands out against a release reached by knowledge without a giver

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools before a king and assembly, with stakes for the loser; distinct from vaadham, the alchemy of the Siddhars
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam title names it (புத்த வாதச் சருக்கம்); the id follows earlier chapters, since vaadham is taken

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: earlier chapters of this sarukkam (478, 484); this chapter says பிண்டம் (636, 640)

new_concepts.gloss: the tales of the Buddha's former births as a Bodhisattva, told chiefly of his gifts of body, family and life
new_concepts.label_source: neelakesi 212 (சாதகம்); here the gifts of eyes (641, 653) and the hare birth (649)

new_concepts.gloss: a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance (பொருள், குணி) that bears it

source_issues: 636, 650, 652, 655, 656 line 2: the old encoding • for ஃ was repaired in the core.
639 line 4 and 654 line 4: a TSCII leftover was repaired (ேரி); 639 line 1 சொன்னேற்கு (first person) sits oddly in the sense.
655 line 3: புத்த£ர் carries the non-Tamil character £ (U+00A3); probably புத்தர் or a vocative புத்தீர்.
655-658: many TSCII leftovers were repaired by the build (ி, ா); readings follow the repaired text.
657 line 4: a stray space before the final full stop (என்றான .).
658 line 4: நோழையும் is not a known name or word; it may be a corruption of a name for Neelakesi (as நீலையும்).
647: in short lines, unlike the four-foot lines around it; it may be a quoted saying or a damaged verse.
648 lines 2-3 and 651 line 4 (உலங்கருவாமே) are obscure and may be corrupt.
636-640 and 645-656: no speech verb names the speaker; Neelakesi is taken as speaker from the run of the argument, the Buddha in 642-644 from என்றான் and the vocative நறுநுதலாய்.
